sections.d: อ่านบทความวิชาการแล้วตอบคำถาม 9 ข้อ

x: A plant that cannot walk must still find new ground. If every seed fell beneath its parent, seedlings would compete with the adult for light and water, and a single disease could destroy an entire family at once. Dispersal — the movement of seeds away from the parent plant — is therefore not a luxury but a requirement, and flowering plants have evolved a striking range of methods to achieve it.

The cheapest method is wind. Dandelion and willow seeds carry hairs that slow their fall, allowing a light breeze to carry them for kilometres. The cost is precision: the great majority of wind-borne seeds land in places where they cannot grow. Plants that rely on wind compensate by producing seeds in enormous numbers and keeping each one very small, which limits the food supply the seedling can carry with it.

Animals offer the opposite trade-off. A fleshy fruit is expensive to build, but a bird that swallows it may deposit the seed several kilometres away, often in a spot already enriched by droppings. Because the animal is choosing where to travel, the seed is more likely to arrive somewhere plants can live. Some species go further and produce seeds with hooks that catch on fur; these travel without the plant having to provide any food at all, though they reach only animals that pass close by.

A few plants dispense with outside help. The squirting cucumber builds up pressure inside its fruit until the seeds are ejected several metres, and certain pine cones open only after fire has passed, releasing seeds onto ground that is briefly free of competitors. Such mechanisms are precise but short-range. Botanists therefore describe dispersal as a series of compromises between distance, cost and the chance of landing somewhere useful — a set of pressures that explains why closely related plants growing in different habitats often disperse in quite different ways.

items.q: What does the passage mainly explain?
c: Why seeds need water to germinate.

sections.d: อ่านบทความวิชาการแล้วตอบคำถาม 9 ข้อ

p.t: The Long Argument About Cave Painting
x: When drawings of bison and horses were first reported from caves in northern Spain in 1880, most scholars refused to accept them. The paintings seemed too accomplished to belong to people who had used stone tools, and one prominent critic suggested that a modern artist had produced them for money. Only in 1902, after similar images had been found in several French caves under layers of undisturbed deposit, did the scientific community accept their age.

Dating remains difficult. The pigments themselves are mineral and cannot be dated directly, so researchers rely on charcoal used in black outlines, on the calcite crusts that grow slowly over a painted surface, and on objects left on the cave floor. Each method has limits: charcoal may come from wood already old when it was burned, and crusts give only a minimum age, since a painting must be older than anything covering it.

Interpretation is harder still. The nineteenth-century view, that the images were simply decoration, is now rejected: the deepest and least accessible chambers, which nobody could live in, are often the most heavily painted. One long-popular alternative held that the paintings were a kind of hunting magic intended to guarantee success. That explanation has weakened as counts have accumulated, because the animals shown do not match the bones found in the same caves. At one well-studied site, reindeer make up the overwhelming majority of the bones but appear in only a handful of images.

Most researchers now accept that no single explanation will cover every site, and some argue that the search for one meaning is itself a modern habit. What the caves do show, uncontroversially, is planning: pigments were carried in, scaffolding was built for high surfaces, and in several caves the same conventions for drawing a particular animal recur across chambers hundreds of metres apart, which suggests that the images were made within a shared tradition rather than by isolated individuals.

c: The paintings seemed too skilful for people who used stone tools.
No animals matching the images were known.
The caves were too difficult to reach.
The pigments were of modern manufacture.

That every site has the same meaning.
That the paintings were made by one artist.
items.ex: ตอบข้อ 2 — บทความใช้คำว่า uncontroversially กับหลักฐานเรื่องการวางแผน คือขนสีเข้าไป สร้างนั่งร้าน และใช้แบบแผนการวาดสัตว์ชนิดเดียวกันซ้ำ ๆ ในห้องที่ห่างกันหลายร้อยเมตร · ข้อ 1 และ 3 เป็นการตีความที่บทความบอกว่ายังไม่ลงตัว · ข้อ 4 ขัดกับคำว่า shared tradition

items.q: What does the recurrence of the same drawing conventions in distant chambers suggest?
c: The images belonged to a shared tradition rather than isolated individuals.
The chambers were painted on the same day.
The artists copied paintings from another cave.
Only one chamber was used at a time.
items.ex: ตอบข้อ 1 — บทความสรุปตรงว่า suggests that the images were made within a shared tradition rather than by isolated individuals · ข้อ 2 และ 4 ไม่มีข้อมูลเรื่องเวลา · ข้อ 3 เป็นการอนุมานเกินกว่าที่บทความรองรับ
